A1.title: High-quality adult CPR with bag-valve-mask ventilation and defibrillator hand-off

items.text: Confirms scene safety, wears PPE (gloves ± eye protection), and identifies their role.
Checks responsiveness, breathing, and carotid pulse (≤10 s); identifies cardiac arrest and calls the resuscitation team, and for a defibrillator.
Positions patient supine on a firm surface, exposes the chest, and adjusts bed height for effective compressions.
Start chest compressions immediately: place one hand’s heel on the lower half of the sternum, arms straight, shoulders over hands.
Delivers 100–120 compressions/min, 5–6 cm deep, with full recoil (confirmed by manikin feedback).
Keeps every interruption in compressions ≤10 s and keeps compression fraction as high as possible (educational target ≥ 60% on manikin data).

Open the airway (head-tilt–chin-lift; jaw thrust). Ventilate with a BVM and 15 L/min oxygen: 30 compressions to 2 breaths before an advanced airway; each breath ~1 second, with visible chest rise. Avoid hyperventilation.
Uses a two-person BVM seal technique when a second rescuer is available.
Attaches AED/defibrillator pads as soon as available with minimal interruption.
Confirms rescuers are clear (verbal and visual check; oxygen device away from chest) before rhythm analysis and shocks.
Resumes compressions immediately after the shock or 'no shock advised' message.
Swaps compressors about every 2 minutes (or sooner if fatigued) with ≤10 s pause.
Uses closed-loop communication: calls out cycle count/time and gives compression and ventilation feedback to the team leader.
Verbalizes post-event actions: ROSC check, documentation of times/events, equipment cleaning and restocking.

B1.title: ECG rhythm recognition and safe manual defibrillation / synchronized cardioversion

items.text: Powers on and checks defibrillator/monitor and selects monitoring lead.
Prepares chest (dry, remove medication patches, avoid pacemaker/ICD site) and applies pads correctly (anterolateral or anteroposterior) with firm contact.
Continues high-quality CPR while the defibrillator is prepared; pre-shock pause kept as short as possible (≤10 s).
Interprets practice rhythm strips: at least 2/3 correct and 100% correct for shockable (VF/pVT) vs non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
Distinguishes pulseless from perfusing rhythm and artifact from VF (checks leads, pads, patient) and states the finding aloud.
Requests/confirms shock order from physician or team leader per local policy and repeats it back.
Selects the correct mode (UNSYNCHRONIZED for VF/pVT) and energy per manufacturer or local protocol; use maximum available if unknown.
Charge the defibrillator, announcing “charging”; continue compressions while it charges if feasible.
Performs a safety check—'I am clear, you are clear, everybody clear'—visually sweeping and moving oxygen away before shocking.
Delivers shock on order and immediately resumes compressions for 2 minutes without a pulse or rhythm check.

Demonstrates synchronized cardioversion for unstable tachycardia with a pulse: confirms order and sedation plan, selects SYNC, verifies R-wave markers, clears, delivers the ordered shock, and rechecks rhythm.
Records shock number, energy, time and rhythm before/after on the event record.
Post-use: removes pads, cleans device, restocks pads/paper, reports any fault, confirms device ready.

C1.title: Airway support: adjuncts, bag-valve-mask ventilation, advanced airway assistance and waveform capnography

items.text: Verifies indication, applies PPE, and checks that suction, oxygen (15 L/min), BVM with reservoir, adjuncts, and capnography are present and working before manipulating the airway.
Opens the airway (head-tilt chin-lift; jaw thrust if trauma suspected).
Suctions the oropharynx under direct vision (≤10 s per pass) and removes visible foreign matter.
Measures and inserts an OPA correctly - only in an unresponsive patient with no gag reflex.
Measures, lubricates and inserts an NPA when gag reflex is present; verbalizes cautions (suspected skull-base fracture, coagulopathy).
Ventilates with BVM: good mask seal, 15 L/min O2, ~1 s per breath, visible chest rise, 30:2 before advanced airway, no hyperventilation.
Prepares equipment to assist an advanced airway (ETT/SGA) on physician request: laryngoscope check, cuff test, stylet, syringe, tube holder, two suction units, capnography line.
Assists intubation/SGA placement with minimal CPR interruption (≤10 s), pre-oxygenation, and equipment passing on request.
Confirms placement with waveform capnography plus chest rise/auscultation; states that an absent waveform means the tube is not in the trachea until proven otherwise.
Secures the device, records depth and connects ventilation at 1 breath every 6 s during CPR without pausing compressions.
Reassesses after each intervention and troubleshoots deterioration using DOPE (displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment).
Documents device, size, depth, time, and ETCO2, and reports to leader using closed-loop communication.

C2.title: Vascular access (IV/IO) and emergency medication preparation and administration during cardiac arrest

items.text: Receives the (verbal) physician order per local policy, verifies patient identity and allergies, and reads the order back.
Performs hand hygiene, applies PPE, and gathers equipment (cannula ≥18G, flushes, securement, IO kit).
Selects a suitable large vein (antecubital/forearm), applies tourniquet and attempts IV access first.
Cleans skin with chlorhexidine, inserts cannula aseptically, confirms flashback and flush without infiltration, and secures the line.
Recognizes failed or non-feasible IV access and proceeds to IO per local policy/order: site, device use, confirmation of placement, flush.
Prepares drug: checks label, concentration, and expiry, calculates and draws up the correct dose (e.g., epinephrine 1 mg; amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg; lidocaine per formulary).
States drug, dose and route aloud, receives confirmation and announces 'given' with the time (closed-loop).
Administers IV/IO push followed by a flush (≥ 20 mL) and limb elevation without interrupting compressions.
Tracks timing: announces next epinephrine due (every 3-5 min) and the amiodarone/lidocaine sequence as ordered.
Applies sharps safety: no recapping, immediate disposal; IO device and needles disposed of safely.
Monitors line patency, infiltration, and rhythm after drugs and reports to leader.
Documents drug, dose, route, site, time, and who administered.

TA.title: Trauma primary survey: exsanguination check, airway assessment, and cervical spine protection

items.text: Prepares before arrival: PPE, team roles confirmed, airway/suction/collar/oxygen/monitor equipment checked, pre-arrival information received.
Identifies exsanguinating external hemorrhage ('x') on arrival and applies immediate direct pressure/tourniquet before airway work.
Maintains manual in-line stabilization (MILS) of the cervical spine throughout airway assessment, or ensures a team member does.
Assesses airway: speaks to patient, looks and listens for secretions, blood, vomit, stridor, voice change, facial/neck trauma, burns.
Opens airway with jaw thrust while maintaining MILS (head-tilt chin-lift only if the airway cannot otherwise be opened).
Suctions under direct vision and removes visible foreign matter.
Inserts OPA or NPA as indicated (NPA caution with midface/skull-base fracture).
Applies high-flow oxygen by NRB mask (15 L/min) and attaches SpO2 (± ETCO2) monitoring.
Anticipates a difficult airway: alerts physician early, prepares airway equipment/drugs on request and assists with MILS during intubation.
Applies correctly sized rigid cervical collar (or spinal motion restriction per local protocol) with no neck movement; MILS maintained until secured.
Takes part in a coordinated log-roll/transfer on the leader's commands, protecting airway and spine.
Reassesses airway after every intervention and reports to leader in closed loop ('airway patent, MILS maintained').
Documents arrival time, airway interventions, collar and hemorrhage-control times.

TB.title: Trauma breathing assessment and recognition/management of life-threatening chest injuries (B)

items.text: Exposes chest and assesses breathing: inspection, auscultation, palpation, respiratory rate, SpO2, work of breathing, tracheal position, JVD, subcutaneous emphysema.
Recognizes life-threatening chest injuries from case cards: tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest.
Applies and titrates high-flow oxygen; monitors SpO2 and ETCO2.
Suspected tension pneumothorax: calls the trauma leader immediately, prepares and assists with decompression on physician order, does not wait for imaging.
Open pneumothorax: applies occlusive dressing sealed on three sides (or vented chest seal per local stock) and monitors for tension physiology.
Massive hemothorax: secures two large-bore IV/IO lines, sends bloods, requests blood products per order, and prepares chest drain set.
Flail chest/rib fractures: supports ventilation, gives analgesia per order, and anticipates deterioration.
Assists chest drain insertion aseptically; sets up underwater seal; checks drainage, swing, and output.
Maintains spinal precautions during positioning and handles sharps safely.
Reassesses breathing after each intervention and reports in closed loop.
Documents findings, interventions, and times.

TC.title: Circulation: hemorrhage control, shock recognition and resuscitation support (C)

items.text: Assesses circulation: heart rate, BP, pulse quality, capillary refill, skin colour/temperature, consciousness; searches for bleeding sources (chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones, external/floor).
Controls external bleeding: direct pressure, wound packing, then tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound tightened until bleeding stops; records tourniquet time.
Recognizes possible pelvic injury and applies (or assists in applying) a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters on leader's instruction.
Establishes two large-bore IV lines (≥18G) or IO access and takes bloods (group/crossmatch and other tests per order).
Classifies shock severity from case data (hemorrhage class I-IV) and names non-hemorrhagic causes (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, neurogenic).
Supports resuscitation per physician order: limited warmed crystalloid, early blood products/massive transfusion activation, TXA per order and local protocol; performs two-person product check.
Applies warming measures: fluid warmer, removes wet clothing, blankets/forced-air warming.
Monitors continuously: ECG, SpO2, BP every 5 min, urine output (catheter per order and contraindications).
Reassesses response to resuscitation (responder, transient responder, non-responder) and reports to leader.
Anticipates definitive care (CT, theatre, IR, transfer) and prepares patient and documents.
Documents tourniquet time, products, TXA time, volumes, and vital signs.

TD.title: Disability, exposure, hypothermia prevention, reassessment and structured handover (D-E)

items.text: Assesses consciousness: AVPU then GCS (E, V, M) with correct component and total scores.
Checks pupils (size, symmetry, reactivity) and gross limb movement/sensation.
Measures capillary blood glucose in any patient with altered consciousness.
Recognizes signs of raised ICP or neurological deterioration (GCS fall ≥2, unilateral dilated pupil, Cushing response) and escalates immediately.
Maintains spinal motion restriction and recognizes signs of spinal cord injury.
Exposes patient fully for head-to-toe inspection and log-roll examination of the back while preserving dignity and evidence.
Prevents and treats hypothermia: removes wet clothing, applies warm blankets/forced-air warming, warmed IV fluids, warm room; measures core temperature.
Gives analgesia/sedation only per physician order and monitors response.
Repeats ABCDE reassessment after each intervention or change in condition, and at least every 5 minutes.
Delivers structured handover (SBAR/MIST-adapted): identification, mechanism, injuries, signs and vital-sign trends, treatment and times given, pending needs.
Uses closed-loop communication: invites and answers questions and confirms receiver's understanding.
Completes trauma flowsheet documentation accurately.

OSCE-1.title: Cardiac arrest: ventricular fibrillation with return of spontaneous circulation

items.text: Recognizes arrest, starts CPR and allocates roles within 1 minute.
Prioritizes defibrillation: confirms rhythm, gives shock order promptly and checks safety.
Directs ACLS algorithm: access, epinephrine timing, antiarrhythmic per physician/protocol.
Considers reversible causes (Hs and Ts) and requests ECG/laboratory tests.
Manages post-ROSC priorities (SpO2, MAP ≥ 65, 12-lead, glucose, temperature) and gives SBAR handover.
Opens airway and ventilates by BVM with 15 L/min O2: visible chest rise, 30:2, no hyperventilation.
Delivers 1 breath every 6 s after advanced airway without pausing compressions.
Prepares/assists advanced airway with pauses ≤10 s.
Confirms placement with waveform capnography and reports ETCO2 values.
Titrates oxygen after ROSC to target SpO2 and reports.
Establishes IV (or IO per policy) promptly after assignment.
Prepares epinephrine/amiodarone correctly with label check and read-back.
Administers drugs at ordered times with flush; announces next epinephrine due.
Maintains aseptic and sharps safety (no recapping).
Records drugs, doses, and times accurately.
Delivers compressions at 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm, full recoil, pauses ≤10 s.
Rotates the compressor every 2 min with minimal pause.
Applies pads correctly and identifies rhythm correctly at each analysis.
Delivers shock with full clear check and resumes CPR immediately.
Records shock number, energy, and time.

common.text: Uses closed-loop communication (call-out, repeat-back, confirmation) for every order and finding.
Maintains situational awareness: reassesses after each intervention and reports changes to the leader.
Demonstrates professional and safe behavior: standard precautions, sharps safety, respect for team and patient dignity, speaks up about safety concerns.

OSCE-1.candidate_instructions: You are part of the emergency resuscitation team. A 58-year-old man collapsed in the waiting area after 30 minutes of chest pain and has just been brought to the resuscitation bay. A physician is available to give orders. Work as a team using the ACLS approach. You will be assessed individually on your role and as a team.
OSCE-1.setting: ED resuscitation; monitor/defibrillator, adult manikin, crash cart, airway kit, IV/IO supplies.
OSCE-1.presentation: 58-year-old man, history of hypertension and smoking. Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no carotid pulse. Skin pale and cool. Monitor leads not yet attached. No known allergies. Weight ~85 kg.

progressive_info.info: Unresponsive, no pulse, no normal breathing. Monitor not attached.
Pads attached: coarse VF. If CPR not started, assessor prompts. Shock delivered ->> VF persists after 2 min CPR.
Second rhythm check: VF persists. IV access in place (or IO if candidate states IV failed). Epinephrine ordered after initial defibrillation attempts.
Third rhythm check: VF persists ->> shock; amiodarone 300 mg ordered. ETCO2 12 mmHg if airway adjunct/waveform attached.
ROSC: sinus rhythm 98/min, BP 82/50 (MAP ~61), SpO2 92% on BVM, ETCO2 38 mmHg, GCS 3.
Post-ROSC prompts: 12-lead ECG shows anterior ST elevation; glucose 6.4 mmol/L; temperature 36.2 C.

OSCE-1.format: Day 2 - ACLS - cardiac arrest - 8 min scenario + 5 min debrief

OSCE-2.title: Respiratory deterioration progressing to respiratory and cardiac arrest

items.text: Calculates MEWS correctly, recognizes high risk and activates rapid response/senior review.
Directs systematic ABCDE and identifies likely cause(s).
Decides on escalation (NIV/ICU/intubation) and communicates by SBAR to physician/ICU.
Recognizes respiratory arrest/PEA and redirects the team to the ALS algorithm.
Delegates tasks and reassesses after each intervention.
Applies controlled/titrated oxygen per local protocol for suspected hypercapnic COPD.
Positions patient upright, assesses work of breathing, prepares nebulized bronchodilator on order.
Recognizes failing ventilation and starts BVM at 1 breath/6 s when needed.
Sets up NIV/HFNC per physician order and monitors tolerance.
Applies waveform capnography and interprets trend.
Repeats full vital signs and MEWS every 5 min and reports trends.
Obtains ABG/VBG and glucose; discusses results with the physician.
Establishes IV access; prepares ordered drugs with read-back and correct dose.
Applies cardiac monitoring; recognizes bradycardia/hypoxic arrest and alerts leader.
Applies droplet/contact precautions as indicated and sharps safety.
Documents MEWS, calls rapid response, and uses SBAR escalation.
Keeps an accurate timeline of events and drugs.
When PEA occurs: starts compressions immediately (100-120/min, ≥ 5 cm).
Applies pads, identifies non-shockable rhythm and withholds shock.
Rotates the compressor every 2 min and maintains safe technique.

OSCE-2.candidate_instructions: You are part of the rapid response team. A 68-year-old man with COPD and a 3-day cough has become drowsy and breathless in an ED observation bay. A physician is available to give orders. Assess, escalate, and treat as a team. You will be assessed individually on your role and as a team.
OSCE-2.setting: ED observation bay (or ward bed); monitor, adult manikin, O2, nebulizer, BVM, suction, MEWS chart, defibrillator, airway kit.
OSCE-2.presentation: 68-year-old man, known COPD, 3 days of productive cough and fever. Drowsy (responds to voice), tripod position, using accessory muscles, speaking 2-3 words. RR 32, HR 122, BP 148/86, SpO2 84% on room air, temperature 38.6 C, glucose 7.8 mmol/L. Educational MEWS= 8; use the MOH chart in the real setting.

progressive_info.info: RR 32, SpO2 84% RA, HR 122, BP 148/86, T 38.6 C, responds to voice. Wheeze and coarse crackles.
After oxygen and nebulizer: SpO2 88%, RR 36, drowsy (responds to pain). ABG: pH 7.21, PaCO2 78 mmHg.

If no escalation/NIV: SpO2 76%, RR 8, HR 48.
If NIV/BVM started appropriately: SpO2 90%, HR 110.
If ventilation is inadequate: apnea, then pulseless PEA at 40/min.
After 2 min CPR and epinephrine, ROSC (HR 96, BP 90/55) - or time ends with CPR ongoing if delayed.

OSCE-2.format: Day 2 - ACLS / rapid response - respiratory deterioration - 8 min scenario + 5 min debrief

OSCE-3.title: Hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock after motorcycle crash

items.text: Activates trauma team, allocates roles and receives pre-arrival information.
Prioritizes hemorrhage control first, then ABCDE order.
Coordinates blood-product activation, TXA (per order) and escalation to theatre/IR.
Recognizes response/non-response and revises plan.
Delivers structured handover to the receiving team.
Maintains MILS and airway patency with high-flow oxygen.
Assesses breathing (RR, SpO2, chest exam) and excludes chest source.
Applies cervical collar/spinal motion restriction per protocol.
Anticipates airway compromise and prepares RSI equipment if ordered.
Reports breathing findings in closed loop.
Applies tourniquet correctly (position, tightness) and records time.
Applies pelvic binder correctly at greater trochanters.
Establishes two large-bore IV/IO lines and draws bloods.
Prepares/administers blood products with two-person check, warmer, and limited crystalloid.
Monitors response (BP, HR, bleeding) and reports.
Assesses GCS, pupils and glucose.
Exposes fully and log-rolls safely with dignity.
Prevents/treats hypothermia (remove wet clothes, warmers, temperature).
Repeats ABCDE reassessment after each change.
Keeps an accurate timeline (tourniquet time, TXA, products).

OSCE-3.candidate_instructions: You are a member of the trauma team. A 28-year-old man has arrived by ambulance after a motorcycle crash. A trauma physician is available for orders. Perform the primary survey and resuscitation as a team. You will be assessed individually on your role and as a team.
OSCE-3.setting: Trauma bay: trauma manikin, monitor, tourniquet, pelvic binder, IV/IO supplies, blood-product simulation, warmers, airway trolley.
OSCE-3.presentation: 28-year-old man, helmet removed by paramedics. Pale, sweaty, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). HR 132, BP 84/50, RR 28, SpO2 94% on room air, capillary refill 4 s, temperature 35.4 C. Brisk arterial bleeding from open left femur fracture; physician reports pelvic instability. Chest clear bilaterally. Weight ~80 kg. No known allergies.

progressive_info.info: Arrival: bleeding from left thigh soaking dressings; HR 132, BP 84/50.

If tourniquet and binder applied and bloods/IV started: HR 122, BP 92/56. 
If not controlled: BP 74/40, GCS 12.

Physician orders blood products and TXA;
 If delivered with warmer: HR 112, BP 100/62. Temp 35.0 C unless warming started.
Transient responder; surgeon requests theatre transfer. GCS 14; glucose 6.1 mmol/L.
Scenario ends with handover to the theatre team.

OSCE-3.format: Day 3 - Trauma 360 - shock - 8 min scenario + 6 min debrief per team

OSCE-4.title: Major trauma: tension pneumothorax, head injury and hypothermia

items.text: Activates the team, leads ABCDE in order, and announces priorities.
Recognizes tension pneumothorax and requests immediate decompression.
Recognizes head injury progression and plans CT/specialist input after stabilization.
Ensures hypothermia prevention and analgesia plan.
Delivers structured handover to CT/ICU team.
Maintains MILS with jaw thrust, suction, and adjunct as needed.
Applies high-flow oxygen and recognizes respiratory compromise.
Prepares and assists with decompression and chest drain aseptically with sharps safety.
Reassesses breathing after decompression and reports.
Prepares for intubation (GCS <=8) on request and uses capnography.
Controls external bleeding and identifies shock signs.
Establishes two large-bore IV/IO lines and draws bloods.
Maintains perfusion per physician targets and avoids hypotension in head injury.
Monitors ECG/BP and recognizes resolution of obstructive shock after decompression.
Uses read-back for drugs/fluids/blood products.
Assesses GCS (correct E/V/M), pupils and glucose.
Recognizes falling GCS/pupil change and escalates; positions head-up with spinal precautions.
Exposes fully and prevents hypothermia.
Repeats ABCDE reassessment after each change.
Keeps an accurate timeline.

OSCE-4.candidate_instructions: You are a member of the trauma team. A 40-year-old man has arrived after a high-speed road traffic collision. A trauma physician is available for orders. Perform the primary survey and resuscitation as a team. You will be assessed individually on your role and as a team.
OSCE-4.setting: Trauma bay: trauma manikin, monitor, decompression and chest drain trainers, airway trolley, warmers.
OSCE-4.presentation: 40-year-old man, front-seat passenger, unrestrained. GCS 10 (E3 V3 M4), RR 36, SpO2 86% on room air, HR 122, BP 92/58, trachea deviated to the left, absent breath sounds right chest, subcutaneous emphysema, scalp laceration, temperature 34.8 C, glucose 6.0 mmol/L.

progressive_info.info: Arrival: distress, SpO2 86%, absent right breath sounds, deviated trachea.

If decompression requested and assisted: SpO2 95%, HR 104, BP 110/70. 
If delayed: SpO2 78%, BP 76/40.
Chest drain prepared; drainage 300 mL blood. Temp 34.5 C unless warming started.
GCS falls to 8, right pupil 5 mm sluggish; physician considers intubation and CT.
Scenario ends with handover to CT/ICU team.

OSCE-4.format: Day 3 - Trauma 360 - major trauma - 8 min scenario + 6 min debrief per team
